title: Find the Distance Value Between Two Arrays
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair directly versus sorting arr2 once and binary searching the closest candidate per arr1 element.

content.title: Find the Distance Value Between Two Arrays

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integer arrays arr1 and arr2, and an integer d, return the number of elements in arr1 such that there is NO element in arr2 within a distance d of it (meaning, for every element y in arr2, the absolute difference between them is strictly greater than d).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","arr1, arr2, d"],["Output","The count of arr1 elements with no arr2 element within distance d"],["Goal","Check each arr1 element efficiently, without comparing it against every arr2 element directly"],["Constraints","1 <= arr1.length, arr2.length <= 500; 0 <= d <= 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The SAME arr2 is checked against every arr1 element","Sort arr2 once, and reuse that sorted order for every check"],["\"No element within distance d\" means checking the CLOSEST arr2 value","Binary search for the nearest candidate in the sorted array"]]}

blocks.text: For each element in arr1, check whether every element in arr2 is more than d away from it; count how many elements in arr1 satisfy this "no close neighbor" condition.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Isolated Houses Far From Any Fire Station
blocks.text: Picture a set of houses (arr1) and a set of fire stations (arr2), and needing to count how many houses have NO fire station within a certain safe distance d, meaning every station is too far away to help quickly.

blocks.caption: Sort arr2 once; binary search finds the closest candidate for each arr1 element

blocks.text: For 4: closest values in arr2 are 1(diff 3) and 8,9,10(diff>=4), none within 2. For 5: same, none within 2. For 8: 8 itself is in arr2, diff 0, so it FAILS. Only 4 and 5 qualify, giving 2.
Before checking every arr1 element against every arr2 element directly, notice that sorting arr2 once lets binary search quickly find the closest candidate for each arr1 element.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An arr1 element x fails the condition (has a close neighbor) if ANY arr2 element falls within [x minus d, x plus d].

Observation 2: If arr2 is sorted, the elements closest to x are found directly with binary search, specifically the first element at least x minus d.

Observation 3: If that closest candidate (or the absence of one) falls outside [x minus d, x plus d], then x has no close neighbor and qualifies.

Observation 4: Sorting arr2 once, up front, lets every arr1 element be checked in O(log(arr2 length)) instead of O(arr2 length).
This leads to sorting arr2 once, then for every arr1 element, binary searching for the first candidate at least x minus d, and checking whether it falls outside the [x minus d, x plus d] window.
For every arr1 element, check every arr2 element directly for closeness.

items: For every x in arr1, check every y in arr2.
If any y is within d of x, x fails the condition.
Count every x that has no such close y.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every arr1 element is compared against every arr2 element directly, with no reuse of prior comparisons.
The same arr2 is re-scanned in full for every single arr1 element.

blocks.text: Limitation: since the same arr2 is checked against every arr1 element, sorting it once and reusing that order via binary search would avoid re-scanning it in full each time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-scanning arr2 per element is wasteful: arr2 never changes, so preparing it once (by sorting) lets every later check be much faster.

What sorting enables: binary search for the smallest arr2 value at least x minus d, the natural starting point for checking nearby values.

How to confirm no close neighbor exists: if that candidate does not exist, or its value exceeds x plus d, then no arr2 element falls in the danger zone.

The core idea: sort arr2 once, then binary search the closest candidate for every arr1 element in O(log(arr2 length)).

Sort arr2 once. For each x in arr1, binary search for the first arr2 element at least x minus d. If no such element exists, or that element is greater than x plus d, then x has no close neighbor, and counts toward the answer.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: sort arr2 once, binary search the closest candidate per element

blocks.text: Once arr2 is sorted, the smallest element at least x minus d is found directly via binary search; if that element (or the fact that none exists) confirms no arr2 value falls within [x minus d, x plus d], then x truly has no close neighbor. This check costs O(log(arr2 length)) per arr1 element, instead of a full O(arr2 length) scan.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((arr1.length plus arr2.length) log(arr2.length)), sorting once plus one binary search per arr1 element.
Space: O(arr2.length) for the sorted copy.

blocks.text: Find the Distance Value Between Two Arrays is a direct "sort once, binary search repeatedly" optimization: since arr2 never changes, preparing it once turns every later closeness check from a full scan into a fast binary search.

items: Re-sorting arr2 inside the loop over arr1, instead of sorting it once outside the loop.
Checking only one neighboring candidate instead of confirming both the found candidate and the fact that no smaller candidate could also be within range.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["d = 0","An arr1 element only fails if it exactly matches some arr2 element."],["arr2 is empty (though constraints guarantee at least 1 element)","Every arr1 element would trivially qualify."]]}

blocks.text: Pointing out that arr2 is fixed across every check, so sorting it once amortizes the cost across all of arr1, demonstrates recognizing the repeated-query structure clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the same arr2 is checked repeatedly", think: sort it once, and binary search for each arr1 element instead of a full scan.

How would you find the SPECIFIC arr1 elements that qualify, not just the count?
Any "sort once, binary search repeatedly" optimization for a fixed reference array checked against many queries.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(arr1.length times arr2.length) time. The optimized sort-plus-binary-search approach runs in O((n+m) log m) time. Both use O(m) or O(1) space respectively.

items: Pattern: sort a fixed reference array once, then binary search it repeatedly for each query.
Core Idea: sort arr2, then for each arr1 element, binary search for the closest candidate at least x minus d, and confirm it (or its absence) falls outside the danger zone.
Time: O(arr1.length times arr2.length) for the brute force, O((n+m) log m) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(m) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: since arr2 is fixed across every check, sorting it once amortizes the preparation cost across all of arr1.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, standard "sort once, binary search per query" optimization.
One line memory trick: sort the fixed array once, binary search the closest candidate per query.
